title: Странное настроение Шефа  (The Chef's Strange Mood)

segments.t: In the staff corridor, Senya and Fedya trade guesses about what was said the night before, right until Chef Barinov storms past yelling at them to get back to work. Fedya declares he is tired of guessing what is wrong with the Chef and decides he is simply crazy.
Я не понял, девочки, вы что, на гособеспечении?
Я уже задолбался угадывать, что с ним.
Давай примем, что он просто псих.
Alright, let's go through it step by step in English.
'Did you tell her yesterday?' Senya probes frankly on the spot, linking "vchera" ("yesterday"), "skazal" ("said"), and "ty" ("you") in one brisk exchange.
'I told her...' Fedya sustains a pointed attitude with Senya, joining "skazal" ("said") to "ya" ("I") so every word pulls its weight.
'Sun. Transformer.' Senya maintains an easygoing tone at this moment, putting "solntse" ("sun") alongside "transformator" ("transformer") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Wait, what did he even say?' Fedya tests boldly as they speak, combining "skazal-to" ("said") and "chto" ("what") so the key meaning lands right away.
'Oh, what a guy.' Senya shows an unhurried course toward Fedya, joining "akh" ("ah, oh") to "chergin" ("Churchill") so every word pulls its weight.
'Something about love, probably.' Fedya adopts a measured style with Senya, building the phrase around "lyubov" ("love") and "navernoye" ("probably") for a crisp, natural delivery.
Я не понял, девочки, вы что, на гособеспечении?

'I do not get it, girls, are you on state welfare or what?' Senya probes quietly with Fedya now, building the phrase around "ponyal" ("understood") and "devochki" ("girl's") for a crisp, natural delivery.
'Get to work fast, you stumps!' Fedya maintains a serious view right away, anchoring the Russian line on "bystro" ("quickly") and "rabotat" ("to work") without extra filler.
'What is wrong with him today?' Senya challenges bluntly without hesitation, weaving "chto" ("what") together with "nim" ("him") just the way native speakers do.
Я уже задолбался угадывать, что с ним.

'I am sick and tired of guessing what is wrong with him.' Fedya brings a sharp note beside Senya, putting "uzhe" ("already, now") alongside "zadolbalsya" ("to get fed up") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
Давай примем, что он просто псих.
'Let us just accept that he is simply nuts.' Senya sets a measured attitude right away, weaving "davay" ("let's") together with "primem" ("to receive") just the way native speakers do.
'Go knock on your own head.' Fedya favors a lively stance beside Senya, weaving "golove" ("the head") together with "postuchi" ("to knock") just the way native speakers do.
Я не понял, девочки, вы что, на гособеспечении?
Я уже задолбался угадывать, что с ним.
Давай примем, что он просто псих.
That wraps up this scene as in the locker room and kitchen corridor, Senya and Fedya try to figure out why Chef Barinov is barking orders and acting even crazier than usual. Until next time!
